html:
The Treaty of Breda, signed on 31 July 1667, ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War. Under it the Dutch kept Suriname, which they had just taken from England, and England kept New Amsterdam, which became New York.

English planters from Barbados had settled Suriname in 1650 and built sugar plantations along its rivers. In February 1667 a Dutch fleet from Zeeland captured the colony and its fort. At Breda each side kept what it held.

The swap looks lopsided now, but in 1667 Suriname's sugar seemed worth more than a fur-trading town on the Hudson. Suriname stayed Dutch until 1975, and Paramaribo became its capital. Its plantations, worked by enslaved Africans brought by the Dutch West India Company and others, also produced the Maroons of the forest.
